In collaborative efforts to maintain regulatory consistency across the EU, Member States work closely with the European Commission, promoting public safety and supporting innovation, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). They provide access to regulatory sandboxes, allowing for experimentation and technological development within the AI sector, while also upholding human rights commitments as per the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

In addition, Member States must adhere to EU laws concerning data processing and police cooperation, which enable them to impose administrative fines when needed. They take a coordinated approach to AI regulation by sharing compliance information and participating in discussions to align national practices with EU standards. Moreover, Member States contribute to market surveillance and regulatory dialogues that advocate for their national interests.

While operating within the EU framework and exercising collective governance, Member States retain certain competencies related to national security and legislative matters specific to their contexts. This autonomy allows them to develop laws concerning worker rights and tailor AI systems to fit their unique circumstances. Overall, Member States are integral components of the EU's institutional fabric, responsible for shaping the regulatory environment surrounding AI and related technologies while balancing diverse responsibilities and commitments within the Union. Additionally, they engage in initiatives to promote socially and environmentally beneficial AI solutions and participate in consultation processes regarding compliance and authorizations, ensuring comprehensive coverage of all regulations, including those on biometric data.<SEP>Member States refer to the countries that are part of the regulatory framework and are implicated in the compliance evaluations of AI systems.<SEP>The Member States contribute to the establishment of testing and experimentation facilities as part of the regulatory framework.

providers of general-purpose AI models
Providers of general-purpose AI models are companies or organizations that develop and offer AI systems capable of performing a wide range of tasks.<SEP>Providers of general-purpose AI models are organizations or businesses that develop and offer AI models for various applications, requiring compliance with specific obligations based on their type and size.

Union copyright law
Union copyright law encompasses legal regulations governing the use and protection of copyrighted material within the Union.<SEP>Union copyright law refers to the legal framework governing copyright within the European Union, influencing compliance obligations for AI model providers.

start-ups
Start-ups are new businesses that fall under the category of SMEs and are similarly considered in the regulatory context.<SEP>Start-ups are newly established companies often looking to innovate, particularly in technology, and are granted simplified compliance measures to promote their development.<SEP>Start-ups are newly established businesses that are often focused on innovation and developing technology, such as AI systems, and typically seek to rapidly grow their market presence.

general-purpose AI models
General-purpose AI models are advanced artificial intelligence systems engineered to perform a diverse array of tasks across various applications. These models are designed for broad use, demonstrating versatility and flexibility in their deployment. They have the capability to learn and adapt based on the data they are trained on, which enables them to handle a wide range of functions beyond predetermined, specific roles.

In addition to their multifaceted applications, general-purpose AI models must comply with various standards and regulations, including those established by the European Union. This compliance involves adherence to necessary codes for safety, performance, and copyright laws. While many of these models are accessible to the public under free and open-source licenses, allowing for broad dissemination and use, they are also subject to specific regulatory constraints that aim to manage potential systemic risks associated with their deployment.

Overall, general-purpose AI models represent a significant advancement in artificial intelligence technology, necessitating responsible governance to address their capabilities and the associated dangers they may pose.

obligations
Obligations refer to the legal responsibilities that entities must adhere to in relation to AI models and their compliance with regulations.<SEP>Obligations refer to the requirements that AI model providers must comply with to ensure ethical standards and regulatory compliance.

nonprofessional or scientific research purposes
Nonprofessional or scientific research purposes denote activities conducted without financial or commercial intent, focusing instead on discovery or academic contributions.

Notified Body
A Notified Body is a specific type of organization recognized under relevant Union legislation, primarily within the European Union (EU), and is responsible for assessing the conformity of products, particularly high-risk AI systems, before they can be marketed. Designated by national authorities in EU member states, Notified Bodies operate under national law and possess legal personality, which enables them to carry out conformity assessments in accordance with various regulatory standards and requirements.

These organizations play a crucial role in ensuring that products meet necessary regulations prior to their release into the market. Notified Bodies assess compliance, issue certifications, and maintain oversight to guarantee adherence to applicable requirements. They are specifically tasked with evaluating high-risk products and systems, ensuring that they conform to essential regulations for safety and effectiveness.

Due to the nature of their work, Notified Bodies are subject to investigation regarding their competence in executing these assessments. This oversight is vital for maintaining high operational standards within the industry and ensuring consumer safety. Overall, Notified Bodies are integral to the regulatory framework that governs the marketing of AI systems and other high-risk products in the EU.<SEP>Notified bodies are organizations designated to assess whether a high-risk AI system conforms to relevant regulations and issue compliance certificates.

Conformity Assessment Activities
Conformity Assessment Activities are tasks conducted by Notified Bodies to evaluate the compliance of high-risk AI systems with necessary regulations and standards.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Activities are the procedures conducted by notified bodies to verify that products, processes, or services meet specified standards.<SEP>Conformity assessment activities refer to the procedures and evaluations conducted by notified bodies to ensure compliance with regulations.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Activities refer to the processes followed by Conformity Assessment Bodies to ensure AI systems meet required standards.

Conformity Assessment Body
A Conformity Assessment Body is a third-party organization responsible for the testing, certification, and inspection of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. This body evaluates whether high-risk AI systems comply with established legal standards and requirements, ensuring their adherence to relevant legislation. Conformity Assessment Bodies perform third-party assessments to validate that AI systems meet regulatory requirements, conducting evaluations to certify compliance with specific standards and regulations relevant to their respective fields. As part of its responsibilities, a Conformity Assessment Body also plays a role in the evaluation process that informs the Commission's decisions regarding the compliance of AI systems with established standards.

Top-Level Management
Top-Level Management refers to the leadership hierarchy within a Conformity Assessment Body that oversees operations and decision-making processes related to conformity assessments.

Personnel
Personnel in a Conformity Assessment Body are the staff responsible for conducting conformity assessment tasks and ensuring compliance with regulations.<SEP>Personnel refers to the staff, committees, and individuals that work within the notified bodies and are crucial for maintaining standards and assessment integrity.<SEP>Personnel refers to the group of individuals engaged in performing tasks in a given organization, emphasizing the need for competent expertise in various fields.

Confidentiality Procedures
Confidentiality Procedures are documented processes that safeguard sensitive information obtained during conformity assessment activities, mandated for Conformity Assessment Bodies.

Cybersecurity Requirements
Cybersecurity Requirements encompass the necessary security measures that Conformity Assessment Bodies must implement to protect the integrity of their assessment processes.<SEP>Cybersecurity Requirements refer to the essential standards and measures that must be met by products with digital elements to ensure their security and compliance with EU legislation.<SEP>Cybersecurity requirements are standards that organizations must meet to protect systems and data during the conformity assessment process.

Liability Insurance
Liability Insurance is protection that Notified Bodies must procure to cover potential legal claims arising from their conformity assessment activities or decisions.<SEP>Liability insurance is a form of coverage that notified bodies must take out for their conformity assessment activities unless covered by the Member State.

Notified Bodies
Notified Bodies are independent organizations designated by national authorities and Member States within the European Union to assess the conformity of high-risk AI systems and other regulated products against established regulatory standards. Their primary responsibilities encompass assessing, approving, and monitoring technical documentation and quality management systems in alignment with Union regulations. 

These organizations are tasked with carrying out thorough conformity assessments while ensuring high professional integrity, competence, and adherence to principles of independence, objectivity, and impartiality. The activities conducted by Notified Bodies are essential for maintaining confidentiality and ensuring all assessment procedures are well-documented.

In addition to their assessment duties, Notified Bodies play a crucial role in verifying compliance with specific standards and regulations, thus contributing to the safety and reliability of high-risk AI systems and other products before they can be marketed within the EU. They are responsible for ensuring that products meet the necessary standards established for market entry, highlighting their importance in the regulatory landscape of high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Notified Bodies are organizations designated to conduct conformity assessments and ensure that specific compliance standards are met for products and systems.<SEP>Notified Bodies are independent organizations designated to evaluate and certify the compliance of high-risk AI systems with regulatory standards.

Judgement or Integrity
Judgement or integrity refers to the principles and standards that guide the operations and assessments made by notified bodies in conformity assessment activities.

Consultancy Services
Consultancy services provided by notified bodies involve offering expertise and guidance in relation to conformity assessments and regulatory compliance.

Article 78
Article 78 outlines confidentiality obligations for the national competent authorities in the performance of their tasks under the regulation.<SEP>Article 78 outlines confidentiality obligations that national competent authorities must follow while performing their regulatory tasks.<SEP>Article 78 refers to a specific provision within Union regulations that governs confidentiality obligations concerning information obtained by various competent authorities during compliance and conformity assessment activities. It outlines requirements for maintaining the confidentiality of sensitive information and trade secrets, particularly in accordance with AI regulations. This article establishes guidelines for ensuring that information obtained by Notified Bodies and national public authorities during assessments and investigations remains protected and handled appropriately.

Moreover, Article 78 specifies confidentiality safeguards for information acquired by market surveillance authorities and mandates confidentiality obligations related to sensitive information gathered during investigations by the Commission. The provisions outlined in Article 78 are set to take effect starting from 2 August 2025. Overall, Article 78 emphasizes the critical importance of confidentiality in the context of regulatory compliance and the safeguarding of sensitive data.

Procedures
Procedures are formalized steps and guidelines that notified bodies must follow to ensure impartiality, confidentiality, and integrity in their assessment activities.<SEP>Procedures refer to the established methods and processes that guide the functioning of the scientific panel, ensuring systematic handling of tasks.

European Standardisation Organisations
European standardisation organisations are entities involved in developing and maintaining standards for various sectors, including those related to AI systems.<SEP>European standardisation organisations are groups that develop and maintain standards for various sectors, including AI systems, and in which notified bodies are encouraged to participate.<SEP>European standardisation organisations are responsible for developing and maintaining standards related to various sectors in the European Union, especially regarding high-risk AI systems.

Professional Integrity
Professional integrity denotes the adherence to ethical standards and practices within the workplace, especially among regulatory bodies.

Technical Personnel
Technical personnel refer to individuals with specialized knowledge and skills in areas such as law, administration, and science needed for effective assessments.

conformity assessment body
A conformity assessment body evaluates the compliance of products or services with established standards, ensuring that they meet specific criteria defined by relevant regulations.

data.entity_name: Official Journal of the European Union
data.content:
Official Journal of the European Union
The Official Journal of the European Union is a publication that disseminates legal texts and regulations adopted by European Union institutions.<SEP>The Official Journal of the European Union is the official publication of the European Union that serves as the formal record of EU regulations, legislation, and other significant documents. It is the designated platform for publishing EU legislation, decisions, notices, and references related to harmonised standards and relevant legislative documents applicable across EU member states. Additionally, it publishes references for certified high-risk AI systems under the pertinent regulations, including their compliance statements. This publication plays a critical role in ensuring transparency and accessibility of EU legislative processes and standards.<SEP>The Official Journal of the European Union publishes legal documents, including regulations and standards that affect all member states, specifically in compliance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012.<SEP>The Official Journal of the European Union is the publication through which the European Union publishes its legal acts, including regulations and standards.

Article 31
Article 31 establishes a comprehensive framework for the requirements and obligations that notified bodies must fulfill to maintain their notification status within the regulatory landscape of the European Union. This article specifies the criteria that these conformity assessment bodies must meet in order to be recognized as competent, ensuring effective oversight of conformity assessment processes as mandated by relevant regulations. It also details the regulatory requirements that govern compliance oversight, which is crucial for maintaining standards in compliance and regulatory practices related to conformity assessment in the EU.

Additionally, Article 31 addresses the specific obligations of notifying authorities and notified bodies regarding market surveillance and compliance assessment of high-risk AI systems. It outlines the conditions that conformity assessment bodies must satisfy before receiving notification, underscoring its significance as a critical component of the legal framework for ensuring rigorous compliance with established standards. Through these provisions, Article 31 plays an essential role in fortifying the integrity of conformity assessment processes across the European market.

Harmonised Standards
Harmonised Standards are technical specifications and standards established within the European Union (EU) to ensure that products and services meet necessary regulatory, safety, and compliance requirements. These standards are developed and recognized by designated organizations, serving as a framework that allows providers to demonstrate conformity with EU legislation. They cover a diverse range of sectors, including those related to artificial intelligence (AI), ensuring that products not only meet specific regulatory mandates but also adhere to safety and effectiveness criteria. Harmonised Standards are crucial in fostering cooperation and consistency across the EU, enabling products and services to achieve compliance with various regulations effectively.<SEP>Harmonised standards provide guidelines that ensure compliance with regulatory requirements for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Harmonised standards are technical standards that comply with European regulations, facilitating the meeting of legal requirements.

Article 31 Requirements
Article 31 Requirements are specific stipulations that entities must meet to demonstrate conformity with EU standards.

AI Office
The AI Office is a dedicated body established to develop expertise and capabilities in AI and to support the implementation of AI regulations within the Union.<SEP>The AI Office is a designated authority within the Union that plays a vital role in overseeing and regulating artificial intelligence (AI) systems, with a particular emphasis on general-purpose AI models. It is tasked with monitoring compliance with established regulations, assessing risks associated with AI technologies, and ensuring adherence to safety standards while protecting individual rights.

One of the core responsibilities of the AI Office is the development and implementation of codes of practice for general-purpose AI models. These codes are designed to reflect international standards and incorporate diverse perspectives, ensuring alignment with Union-level regulations. The Office regularly reviews these codes to maintain compliance and effectiveness in the face of evolving AI technologies.

Functioning as the secretariat for the Board, the AI Office organizes meetings, prepares agendas, and develops methodologies crucial for evaluating AI systems. This evaluation process is essential for verifying that AI technologies meet safety standards and for identifying potential risks within the information society. In addition, the Office coordinates investigations into high-risk AI systems to ensure compliance with EU regulations and engages in collaborative inquiries as necessary.

Collaboration is a fundamental aspect of the AI Office's approach. It actively engages with a broad range of stakeholders, including representatives from the scientific community, industry experts, and civil society, to assess the capabilities and risks posed by AI technologies. This engagement facilitates the establishment of operational thresholds essential for the safe and compliant functioning of AI systems.

Moreover, the AI Office oversees classification rules and compliance procedures related to AI technologies. It develops and recommends model terms for contracts involving high-risk AI systems and contractual terms for providers and third parties involved in compliance efforts. The Office also supports national competent authorities in establishing regulatory frameworks and facilitating regulatory sandboxes, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of AI regulation across various jurisdictions.

Recognizing the complexity of its functions, the AI Office acknowledges the need for additional powers and resources. This acknowledgment underscores its commitment to promoting safety and competence within the regulatory landscape. Through its multifaceted roles, the AI Office diligently works to ensure the safe and responsible use of AI systems, making it a pivotal entity in the governance and oversight of AI technology, particularly in relation to regulations set to take effect from January 24, 2024.<SEP>The AI Office is an organizational entity responsible for overseeing or managing initiatives related to artificial intelligence.<SEP>The AI Office is tasked with overseeing the implementation and compliance related to AI regulations and may request updates to guidelines.<SEP>The AI Office is an entity that may initiate structured dialogue with providers of AI models for information requests.

National Market Surveillance Authorities
National Market Surveillance Authorities are bodies within member states responsible for overseeing regulated credit institutions and ensuring compliance with financial regulations.<SEP>National market surveillance authorities are responsible for the oversight of AI systems at a national level, ensuring compliance and safety.<SEP>National market surveillance authorities are the entities within each Member State responsible for enforcing compliance with the Union harmonisation legislation.

General-Purpose AI Models
General-Purpose AI Models are versatile artificial intelligence systems designed to perform a wide range of tasks without being specifically tailored to any single application. Their broad adaptability and functionality allow them to be applied across various sectors and domains, making them significant advancements within the AI landscape. These models serve as foundational technologies for numerous downstream systems and applications, highlighting their critical role in the evolution of AI.

As General-Purpose AI Models are implemented widely, they come under specific regulatory obligations and compliance measures. Competent authorities oversee their use to ensure adherence to established safety and ethical standards, which are vital for responsible deployment. Evaluations are conducted to assess potential systemic risks associated with these models, particularly when classified as high-risk AI systems. 

In addition to their adaptability, these models have the capability to generate various types of content, including text and images, which creates both opportunities and challenges for creators across multiple fields. Many General-Purpose AI Models are made available under free and open-source licenses, promoting transparency and accessibility in the AI community while balancing innovation with the necessary oversight to mitigate related risks. Overall, General-Purpose AI Models signify a notable evolution in AI technology, combining versatility with a commitment to safety and responsible use.

Compliance Evaluations
Compliance evaluations are processes conducted by market surveillance authorities to assess whether AI systems meet the established regulatory requirements.<SEP>Compliance evaluations assess whether AI systems and models adhere to legal and regulatory requirements.

Cross-Border Cases
Cross-border cases involve regulatory issues that span multiple jurisdictions, requiring cooperation between different national authorities.

mutatis mutandis
Mutatis mutandis is a Latin phrase used in legal and philosophical contexts meaning 'with the necessary changes having been made' or 'the necessary adjustments being made'. It indicates that something remains valid despite changes in circumstances.

European Harmonised Standards
European Harmonised Standards are regulations that provide a framework for compliance for manufacturers and providers within the EU.<SEP>European Harmonised Standards refer to approved protocols that grant presumed conformity for compliance with obligations placed on providers of AI models.

Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
Providers are organizations or entities that develop, market, or use general-purpose AI models and are obligated to ensure safety and compliance.<SEP>Providers of general-purpose AI models are entities responsible for developing, deploying, and maintaining AI systems that serve multiple applications.<SEP>Providers of general-purpose AI models are organizations responsible for creating and managing AI systems that can perform a wide range of tasks and pose systemic risks.<SEP>Providers of General-Purpose AI Models are organizations or entities that develop and supply AI models intended for widespread use in various applications.

Articles 53 and 54
Articles 53 and 54 refer to specific sections of a regulatory framework that outline obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risks.

Article 56
Article 56 pertains to codes of practice that providers can use to demonstrate compliance with obligations until a harmonised standard is published.<SEP>Article 56 refers to a specific regulation within the legal framework governing AI models, which includes codes of practice for compliance.

Systemic Risk
Systemic Risk relates to the potential negative impacts of AI models when they are integrated into broader systems, warranting regulatory obligations.<SEP>Systemic risk refers to the potential for widespread impact on the market and society resulting from the deployment of general-purpose AI models.<SEP>Systemic risk refers to the potential for widespread failure in the financial system, potentially highlighted in evaluations involving AI models.<SEP>Systemic risk refers to the potential for an event or failure in one part of a system, such as AI models, to cause widespread failure or negative impacts on the broader system or society.

Model Evaluation
Model Evaluation is the assessment of the model's performance based on various metrics to determine its effectiveness and reliability.<SEP>Model evaluation involves assessing the AI model's performance and risks using standardized protocols and tools.

Adversarial Testing
Adversarial testing involves evaluating AI models to identify vulnerabilities and ensure they are resilient against malicious inputs.<SEP>Adversarial testing is a method used to identify vulnerabilities in AI models by challenging them with difficult or unexpected inputs.

European Harmonised Standard
A European harmonised standard refers to standards that have been established to ensure compliance with specific regulations and directives within the European Union.

Approved Code of Practice
An approved code of practice is a set of guidelines or standards that organizations are required to adhere to in order to ensure compliance with regulations.

Trade Secrets
Trade Secrets involve practices, designs, formulas, processes, or any type of information that provides a business advantage over competitors.<SEP>Trade secrets refer to confidential business information that provides a competitive edge to a company and is protected under confidentiality obligations.<SEP>Trade secrets encompass confidential business information that is protected under the Directive (EU) 2016/943, preventing unlawful acquisition, use, and disclosure.<SEP>Trade secrets are a form of intellectual property that comprises information that is not generally known or reasonably ascertainable by others, which gives a business a competitive edge.<SEP>Trade secrets are confidential practices, formulas, processes, or various types of information that provide a business with a competitive edge and must be legally protected.

European Data Protection Board
The European Data Protection Board advises on the regulation concerning data protection and privacy in the European Union.<SEP>The European Data Protection Board is responsible for ensuring consistent application of data protection rules across the EU.<SEP>The European Data Protection Board is tasked with ensuring that data protection rules are applied consistently across the European Union.

Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 establishes rules for the processing of personal data by European Union institutions and bodies.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 is a comprehensive legal framework designed to protect personal data within the context of EU institutions and bodies, including the European Commission. It governs the processing of personal data by these entities, ensuring compliance with data protection laws and safeguarding the privacy of individuals. The regulation specifically addresses the rights of individuals concerning how their personal data is processed, promoting transparency and accountability in the management of personal information.

In addition to establishing rules for the secure and lawful handling of personal data, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 facilitates the free movement of such data across the Union. It also provides guidelines for processing personal data in sandbox experimentation environments, ensuring that these processes conform to established data protection standards.

Moreover, this regulation interacts with AI regulations, highlighting its relevance in the evolving landscape of technology and data processing. Overall, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 is critical in protecting individuals' rights regarding their personal data and serves as a foundational element in the EU's commitment to privacy and data protection.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 pertains to the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data by the Union institutions and bodies.

Article 42(1) and (2)
Article 42(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 outlines the consultation process involving the European Data Protection Supervisor and the European Data Protection Board.

18 June 2021
18 June 2021 is the date when the European Data Protection Supervisor and the European Data Protection Board delivered their joint opinion.

Article 79(1)
Article 79(1) is a provision that defines the criteria under which a high-risk AI system is considered to present a risk.<SEP>Article 79(1) pertains to regulations governing the risks presented by high-risk AI systems and the requirements for traceability.

Article 72
Article 72 focuses on post-market monitoring of high-risk AI systems to ensure their safe operation after deployment.<SEP>Article 72 refers to a legislative framework that discusses the requirements for post-market monitoring of high-risk AI systems.

Article 26(5)
Article 26(5) outlines the monitoring requirements for the operation of high-risk AI systems during their lifecycle.

Annex III
Annex III is a crucial segment of regulations governing high-risk artificial intelligence (AI) systems under European Union law. It details the categories and criteria for identifying high-risk AI systems along with the specific compliance measures required for their testing and operation. This section serves as a comprehensive framework that facilitates the classification of AI systems according to their risk levels, which is essential for ensuring their responsible deployment and regulatory scrutiny.

The provisions of Annex III include requirements for transparency and traceability in the operations of high-risk AI systems, emphasizing the need for robust logging capabilities to assist in compliance and evaluation processes. It mandates that systems classified as high-risk must be registered before they can enter the market or be deployed as services, ensuring adherence to high safety and ethical standards.

Furthermore, Annex III outlines the conditions necessary for AI system certifications, which have a validity period of four years and include provisions for re-assessment. It not only catalogues high-risk AI applications but also delineates the relevant assessment obligations that accompany them, as well as the procedures and requirements for demonstrating compliance.

Additionally, Annex III addresses specific legal implications for high-risk AI in areas such as law enforcement, migration, asylum, and border control management. Overall, it represents a vital regulatory framework that defines the appropriate classification of high-risk AI systems, the standards for assessing their risks and impacts, and the operational conditions essential for maintaining regulatory compliance and ethical integrity in the use of AI technologies.<SEP>Annex III outlines specific high-risk AI systems mentioned in the Regulation, detailing their characteristics and usage requirements.

Event Logging
Event logging refers to the capability of high-risk AI systems to automatically record events over their operational lifetime for traceability.

Traceability
Traceability is the property that enables tracking the workflow and decision-making process in high-risk AI systems, facilitating accountability.

Deployer
The Deployer is an entity that cooperates with the Provider in organizing the real-world testing of AI systems, ensuring informed participation.<SEP>The Deployer is defined as a natural or legal person or public authority responsible for implementing and utilizing high-risk AI systems under their authority, with the exclusion of personal non-professional use. This entity plays a crucial role in the deployment process, as it holds legal responsibilities and is tasked with ensuring the safe and effective operation of these systems. The Deployer must possess a thorough understanding of the AI system’s outputs to utilize them appropriately, which is essential for making informed decisions that can significantly affect individuals.

Moreover, the Deployer is required to adhere to risk mitigation guidelines provided by the Provider, ensuring compliance with regulatory measures. This involves adequate training and information dissemination to handle the associated risks effectively. By overseeing the proper use of high-risk AI systems, the Deployer ensures that these technologies are operated within a framework that prioritizes safety and accountability, thus playing an integral role in the responsible deployment of AI. Overall, the Deployer encompasses any individual or organization that operates an AI system under their authority, reinforcing the need for awareness regarding the risks and necessary mitigation measures.<SEP>The deployer is the individual or entity responsible for assessing and managing the risks associated with the use of AI systems.

Public Authority
A public authority is an organization that operates under governmental authority and may deploy AI systems.<SEP>Public authorities are government organizations responsible for safeguarding public interests, including health and safety, within the context of the AI Regulatory Sandbox.<SEP>Public Authority refers to agencies or bodies that deploy AI systems and are responsible for ensuring compliance with AI regulations.

Agency
An agency is a body that can act on behalf of another organization and may deploy AI systems.

Legal Person
A legal person refers to any organization that possesses legal rights and obligations, capable of deploying AI systems.<SEP>Legal persons refer to organizations or entities, such as corporations and governments, that have legal rights and responsibilities.

Natural Person
A natural person is an individual human being, particularly in the context of being assessed for risks related to criminal offenses.<SEP>A natural person refers to an individual human being who can also deploy AI systems under certain conditions.<SEP>Natural persons are individual human beings who possess legal rights and obligations under the law.<SEP>Natural person defines any human individual participating in the testing of AI systems in real-world conditions, with certain rights and responsibilities.

Authority
Authority refers to a person or group having the relevant legal or official power to grant access or make decisions regarding physical spaces.<SEP>Authority refers to the power or right given to deployers to utilize AI systems within a defined scope.

Scientific Panel of Independent Experts
The scientific panel consists of independent experts in the field of AI, tasked with providing expertise and objective assessments.

AI Models
AI Models refer to general-purpose artificial intelligence systems that are designed to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence. These systems can vary in capabilities and applications, encompassing both general-purpose and specialized models. AI Models are governed by specific regulations and are subject to compliance with established codes of practice and standards, ensuring their safe and effective implementation. Additionally, they are composed of algorithms that generate data outputs, including text and images, and are frequently utilized in the automation of content creation. Overall, AI Models highlight the importance of adherence to regulatory obligations for compliance and monitoring, promoting responsible use in various applications of artificial intelligence.<SEP>AI Models refer to specific implementations or designs of AI systems that are subject to regulation under Union Law, especially for ethics and safety purposes.<SEP>AI Models refer to systems that leverage artificial intelligence technologies, specifically general-purpose models that can be utilized across various applications and industries.<SEP>AI models encompass the algorithms and methodologies employed in AI systems, which must comply with specific legal standards.

Independent Experts
Independent Experts are professionals selected based on their expertise in AI, tasked with providing impartial contributions to the regulation enforcement efforts.<SEP>Independent experts are individuals or groups that the AI Office can involve to provide unbiased evaluations of compliance with regulations regarding AI models.<SEP>Independent Experts are professionals with specialized knowledge who can offer their expertise during the creation of AI codes of practice.<SEP>Independent experts are individuals appointed by the Commission to carry out evaluations on behalf of the Commission.

Monitoring Activities
Monitoring Activities involve the processes undertaken by the AI Office and the independent experts to ensure compliance with AI regulations.

AI Systems Regulation
AI Systems Regulation is a comprehensive legal framework designed to govern the assessment and compliance of artificial intelligence technologies across various sectors. It outlines specific cases where AI systems do not pose significant risk of harm, clarifying their intended use and limitations. This set of compliance guidelines establishes transparency obligations for AI systems under both Union and Member State law, ensuring that users and providers understand the functional requirements and responsibilities associated with high-risk AI systems before their introduction to the market.

Furthermore, the AI Systems Regulation specifies rules for the providers and deployers of AI systems within the Union, detailing requirements for transparency and usability, particularly for high-risk applications. It also emphasizes the need for real-time operation of AI systems, highlighting the importance of immediate functionality without significant delays. Overall, the regulation aims to foster safe and responsible AI deployment while upholding user rights and societal standards.

Member State Law
Member State Law consists of national legislations that may impose additional transparency obligations on deployers of AI systems.<SEP>Member State Law refers to the individual laws enacted by countries that are part of the European Union, which must align with EU directives.

Transparency Obligations
Transparency Obligations refer to the requirements established for the disclosure of information related to the use and output of AI systems, ensuring accountability in their deployment.<SEP>Transparency Obligations refer to the requirements for informing individuals about interactions with AI systems.

Deployment of AI Systems
Deployment of AI Systems involves the real-world application and utilization of AI technologies, which must adhere to various legal and regulatory frameworks.

Council
The Council is an organization composed of representatives from Member States, responsible for various legislative and administrative tasks related to the EU.<SEP>The Council, formally known as the Council of the European Union, is a vital institution within the European Union's institutional framework. It represents the governments of the EU member states and plays a key role in the legislative decision-making process. The Council works collaboratively with the European Parliament and the Commission to evaluate, amend, and review legislative proposals, including those concerning regulations on artificial intelligence systems. As a key decision-making body, the Council contributes to shaping EU legislation by considering reports and proposals that impact member states and their governance.<SEP>The Council refers to the Council of the European Union, which, along with the Parliament, plays a key role in the legislative process.<SEP>The Council refers to the Council of the European Union, where member state governments are represented, playing a vital role in decision-making.

Delegated Acts
Delegated Acts refer to legal acts that the European Commission can adopt to supplement or amend non-essential elements of EU legislation.<SEP>Delegated acts are legislative measures that allow the Commission to supplement or amend existing legislative acts.<SEP>Delegated acts are measures adopted by the Commission to modify existing legislation, which includes the power to amend provisions in relation to AI systems.<SEP>Delegated acts refer to measures taken by the Commission to modify existing legislation relating to AI systems and their risk factors.<SEP>Delegated acts are legal acts that allow the European Commission to supplement or amend non-essential parts of legislative acts.

data.entity_name: Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making
data.content:
Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making
The Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making outlines processes for improving the quality of EU legislation.<SEP>This agreement establishes principles for the drafting and adoption of better laws within the European Union.<SEP>This agreement outlines the principles for better legislative practices and is referenced as a guideline for the Commission's consultations.

Article 6
Article 6 is a section of the EU regulation that outlines the classification of AI systems into high-risk and non-high-risk categories.<SEP>Article 6 refers to specific provisions within EU legislation that detail the process and authority for adopting delegated acts.<SEP>Article 6 outlines the classification criteria for AI systems, determining whether they fall under the high-risk category based on their intended purpose.

Article 7
Article 7 outlines additional provisions regarding the delegation of acts by the Commission and the roles of other institutions.

Article 11
Article 11 describes the process for adopting and implementing delegated acts concerning various legislative measures.<SEP>Article 11 refers to a specific regulation detailing how technical documentation must be prepared for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 pertains to implementing acts for artificial intelligence systems, emphasizing the safety components required.

Article 43
Article 43 details the procedures for conformity assessment that must be adhered to for CE marking.<SEP>Article 43 discusses compliance and procedural conditions related to the delegation of powers to the Commission.<SEP>Article 43 is a regulatory provision that outlines the conformity assessment procedures required for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Article 43 refers to a specific provision in EU regulations that addresses the conditions under which high-risk AI systems may be authorized for use.<SEP>Article 43 outlines the conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems as stipulated in the regulation.

Article 47

High-risk AI systems are artificial intelligence systems that pose significant risks to safety or rights, subject to stringent compliance requirements under EU regulations.<SEP>High-risk AI systems are defined as artificial intelligence technologies that present significant potential risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights. The operation of AI systems varies widely, ranging from low-risk applications to those with significant implications for health, safety, and fundamental rights. This regulatory framework is particularly important within the context of European Union compliance standards, where AI systems must adhere to specific regulations regarding data protection, especially since many of these systems process personal data.

AI systems can also influence various aspects of life, including political campaigning and voting behaviors, particularly in the context of elections. Their growing importance extends to accessibility considerations, as they play a role in improving various services and technologies for individuals with different needs.

Section 2
Section 2 of Chapter III is a critical component of the regulatory framework governing artificial intelligence systems, particularly those classified as high-risk. This section outlines detailed requirements and standards that these AI systems must fulfill to ensure compliance and safety within the market. Specifically, Section 2 delineates the safety components that high-risk AI systems are required to incorporate, establishing a clear set of criteria for authorization and compliance. Providers of such systems must adhere to these regulatory requirements as part of the broader EU regulatory framework designed to enhance the safety and reliability of AI technologies.<SEP>Section 2 refers to specific requirements set in the regulation that AI systems must meet to ensure safety and compliance.

EU Legislative Document 2024/1689
The EU Legislative Document 2024/1689 is a legal document related to regulations issued by the European Union in 2024.

Data from Europe
Data from Europe refers to datasets and information released by the European Union pertaining to laws, regulations, and directives.

AI Value Chain
The AI Value Chain refers to the various stages and parties involved in creating AI systems, tools, and services along with the integration and development processes.<SEP>The AI value chain refers to the various stages and roles that contribute to the development, implementation, and management of AI technologies across industries.<SEP>The AI value chain encompasses various stages and responsibilities in the development and deployment of AI technologies, particularly regarding compliance and implementation practices.<SEP>The AI value chain refers to the entire process involved in the development, deployment, and management of AI systems, emphasizing the importance of cooperation among stakeholders.<SEP>The AI value chain encompasses all the stages involved in the development, deployment, and monitoring of AI systems, including cooperation among various stakeholders.

Providers
Providers are entities or individuals responsible for the development, management, and supply of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and components, particularly those classified as high-risk. They play a vital role in ensuring that AI systems meet the mandatory requirements set forth by legislation before being offered in the market. This includes a commitment to compliance with regulatory standards, which is crucial for both high-risk and general-purpose AI systems.

Providers must demonstrate conformity to applicable regulations, which may be requested by competent authorities, and they are accountable for the accurate and appropriate use of AI systems. This accountability extends to the creation and distribution of necessary documentation that is accessible and understandable to users. Providers may also operate in specific sectors, such as financial services, where they must adhere to particular governance and quality management standards.

Furthermore, providers are responsible for establishing and documenting post-market monitoring systems for high-risk AI technologies, which involves ensuring compliance and conducting performance evaluations. Overall, providers are integral to the development and integration of AI technologies, ensuring that they operate within the framework of regulatory compliance while addressing market needs.<SEP>Providers are organizations or entities that develop and supply general-purpose AI models for various uses and applications.<SEP>Providers are entities or individuals that develop high-risk AI systems and are subject to conformity assessments by notified bodies.<SEP>Providers of high-risk AI systems are responsible for ensuring compliance with regulations and taking corrective actions as necessary.

Tools and Services
Tools and services in the context of AI are software applications and support systems that help in the development, training, and deployment of AI models.

Model Training
Model Training is the process of teaching an AI model using data sets to enable it to make predictions or decisions.

Model Testing
Model Testing evaluates the performance and accuracy of an AI model by running it against test data and measuring outcomes.

Integration into Software
Integration into Software refers to the process of incorporating AI components into existing software systems for enhanced functionality.

Written Agreement
A written agreement defines the roles and responsibilities of different parties involved in the testing of AI systems, ensuring accountability and clarity.<SEP>Written Agreement is a formal document outlining the terms and conditions between parties involved in the AI value chain, ensuring clarity and commitment.

Intellectual Property Rights
Intellectual Property Rights protect the creations of the mind, including inventions, literary and artistic works, and symbols.<SEP>Intellectual Property Rights refer to legal protections for creations of the mind, crucial for safeguarding technological innovations and inventions.<SEP>Intellectual property rights encompass the legal rights that protect the creations of the mind, including inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, and symbols, names, and images used in commerce.<SEP>Intellectual property rights protect creations of the mind, such as inventions and trade secrets, which must be considered when publishing lists of AI models.<SEP>Intellectual property rights are legal rights that provide creators protection over their inventions, designs, and artistic works, significant in the context of confidentiality.

The Commission
The Commission is a governing and authoritative body within the European Union responsible for the regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, with a particular emphasis on high-risk applications affecting health, safety, and fundamental rights. It designates general-purpose AI models as presenting systemic risks and is empowered to adopt delegated acts, thereby ensuring proper coordination and collaboration among notified bodies that oversee high-risk AI.

In its regulatory role, the Commission is tasked with assigning identification numbers to these notified bodies and maintaining a public list of them. It plays a critical function in monitoring and regulating emerging technologies, which includes the publication of annual reports concerning biometric identification systems used for law enforcement purposes. The Commission also develops guidance for compliance related to obligations for reporting serious incidents involving AI systems.

Moreover, the Commission is heavily involved in implementing and overseeing regulations concerning content practices, while also fostering initiatives that encourage AI development and data exchange. As the executive branch of the European Union, it is integral to proposing legislation and executing decisions that form the regulatory framework for AI systems. The Commission continuously assesses and amends regulations to uphold transparency and compliance within the sector, ensuring that the guidelines address the needs of various stakeholders, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and public authorities. Overall, the Commission serves as a crucial regulatory entity, overseeing compliance with legal obligations and shaping the landscape for AI technologies in the EU.

Article 5
Article 5 is a crucial component of the regulatory framework concerning artificial intelligence (AI), establishing clear prohibitions related to non-compliant AI practices that must be followed within the market. This article specifically addresses the prohibition of unacceptable AI practices, ensuring that AI systems are developed and operated in a manner that is both safe and ethical.

The provisions outlined in Article 5 detail specific practices that are not permitted under the established regulations, highlighting the need for regular assessments by the Commission to evaluate compliance. Moreover, Article 5 includes stipulations regarding the testing and use of high-risk AI systems, reinforcing the necessity of adhering to safety and ethical standards.

It emphasizes the importance of compliance and accountability in the development and operation of AI systems, making it clear that violations of these regulations are subject to penalties. Furthermore, it mandates that Member States align their practices with these regulations to uphold the integrity of the AI regulatory landscape. Overall, Article 5 serves as a foundational element within this framework, ensuring that ethical standards are maintained in the use of artificial intelligence.

Article 50
Article 50 outlines essential transparency obligations that must be fulfilled by providers and deployers of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It establishes clear requirements for these transparency measures, ensuring that the implementation of AI systems adheres to accountability and ethical standards. Specifically, Article 50 applies to AI systems that require additional transparency measures and is subject to amendments based on evaluations of compliance and effectiveness. Furthermore, it addresses specific compliance requirements and enforcement measures under the broader framework of EU regulations. Organizations implementing AI systems are mandated to comply with these outlined transparency obligations to promote responsible and ethical use of AI technology.<SEP>Article 50 refers to a specific provision of the Regulation concerning high-risk AI systems and their use in decision-making processes.

Article 99
Article 99 refers to a provision within EU regulations that outlines the penalties for non-compliance by providers regarding AI systems.<SEP>Article 99 refers to the penalties related to infringements of the regulation, particularly administrative fines applied by Member States.<SEP>Article 99 stipulates the penalties for providers that fail to comply with the regulatory requirements, emphasizing accountability.

Union agency
A proposed body that may be created to address identified shortcomings in the enforcement of AI regulations.

energy-efficient development of AI models
Energy-efficient development of AI models refers to practices aimed at optimizing AI system performance while minimizing their environmental impact.<SEP>This refers to the regulatory focus on developing AI models in an energy-efficient manner as part of standardisation deliverables.

Article 99(1)
Article 99(1) outlines specific administrative fines applied by Member States for regulatory infringements concerning AI systems.

evaluation
Evaluation refers to the process undertaken by the Commission to assess the functions and effectiveness of the AI Office and other regulatory measures.

standardisation deliverables
Standardisation deliverables encompass the necessary outcomes expected for the development and implementation of AI technologies in compliance with regulations.

environmental sustainability
Environmental sustainability refers to the principles that govern the environmental impact and efficiency of AI systems and their development.

European Economic and Social Committee
The European Economic and Social Committee provides a platform for civil society organizations to express their opinions on EU policies, including those affecting AI systems.<SEP>The European Economic and Social Committee provides opinions on EU legislation, including the assessment of AI-related regulations.

Chapter III, Section 2
Chapter III, Section 2 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 encompasses a comprehensive set of requirements aimed at promoting the responsible application of artificial intelligence (AI) systems while ensuring their alignment with European values. This section outlines specific rules and technical specifications related to the implementation of safety standards for AI systems. It also details the necessary protocols for CE marking, emphasizing the importance of adherence to regulatory compliance to avoid penalties. Furthermore, Chapter III, Section 2 includes classifications for AI systems, encompassing risk assessments that AI systems must undergo to ensure they meet established criteria. Overall, this section serves as a critical component of the legislative framework governing the development and deployment of AI technologies within the European Union.

voluntary codes of conduct
Voluntary codes of conduct are guidelines meant for organizations to adopt best practices in the deployment of AI systems, focusing on ethical standards and sustainability.

2 August 2028
The date by which the Commission is mandated to evaluate the effectiveness of voluntary codes of conduct pertaining to AI systems.

2 August 2031
2 August 2031 is the deadline set for the Commission to carry out an assessment of the AI Regulation enforcement and report the findings.<SEP>The date by which the Commission must assess the enforcement of AI-related regulations and report to relevant EU bodies.
