data.content:
State of Progress in the Information Society
The State of Progress in the Information Society refers to the evaluation of advancements and challenges associated with information technology and governance.

Risk Levels
Risk Levels refer to the evaluations conducted to assess potential hazards associated with AI systems as outlined in the Regulation.

Sectoral Union Harmonisation Legislation
Sectoral Union Harmonisation Legislation refers to laws that aim to standardize regulations across the EU relating to different sectors, affecting AI implementation.

Existing Governance
Existing Governance refers to the current frameworks and structures in place that oversee AI systems and their compliance within the EU.

Enforcement Mechanisms
Enforcement Mechanisms are the strategies and processes put in place to ensure compliance with the AI Regulation.

Authorities Established
Authorities Established refers to the regulatory bodies designated to oversee compliance and enforcement of AI-related laws.

Union Agency
The Union Agency is a proposed regulatory body that would be responsible for resolving enforcement shortcomings identified in the regulation.

General-Purpose AI Model
The General-Purpose AI Model is an advanced type of artificial intelligence designed to perform a wide array of tasks across various applications and domains. These models are recognized for their versatility and are capable of completing diverse functions, making them suitable for a multitude of situations. Given their extensive functionalities, General-Purpose AI Models are subject to regulatory scrutiny to ensure they adhere to compliance protocols aimed at minimizing risks associated with their deployment.

These systems are evaluated for their capabilities and the systemic risks they may pose, with oversight provided by regulatory bodies such as The Commission, which assesses these models based on specific criteria. It is imperative that before their market introduction, General-Purpose AI Models comply with necessary guidelines to guarantee safe and ethical usage, emphasizing the importance of thorough consideration in both their deployment and governance.

While these models hold significant potential for innovation, they also necessitate vigilant management of the risks involved, highlighting the dual responsibility of leveraging their capabilities while addressing the societal implications of their use. Overall, General-Purpose AI Models serve as foundational frameworks adaptable to various applications, underscoring the critical need for careful evaluation and regulation to harness their benefits responsibly.<SEP>The general-purpose AI model refers to an artificial intelligence system designed for various applications, possibly including legal contexts.

Scientific Community
The scientific community includes researchers and experts involved in the study and development of artificial intelligence technologies.

Industry
Industry refers to commercial sectors that are represented in the advisory forum to provide insights into business practices and interests relevant to the Regulation.<SEP>Industry represents various sectors that utilize AI technologies and engage in developing codes of practice as part of regulatory compliance.<SEP>The industry encompasses businesses and enterprises that develop, deploy, or utilize AI systems in various sectors.

Civil Society
Civil society encompasses non-governmental organizations and communities that represent the public interest and contribute to decision-making in the advisory forum.<SEP>Civil society refers to organizations and groups that represent the interests and views of the public concerning the impact of AI technologies.

Threshold
A threshold for cumulative computation is set to determine if a general-purpose AI model presents systemic risks based on its capabilities.

High-Impact Capabilities
High-impact capabilities refer to the advanced functionalities of AI models that can have significant impacts on society or the market.

Floating Point Operations
Floating Point Operations are a measure of computational work done in training AI models, used to determine their potential impact and classification.<SEP>Floating point operations are a measure of computational capacity, used to evaluate the capabilities of general-purpose AI models.

Training Data Set
The training data set consists of data used to train AI models, influencing their performance and capabilities.<SEP>The training data set is a collection of data used to train AI models, influencing their performance, capabilities, and potential biases.

End Users
End users are individuals or organizations that utilize AI models and may be impacted by their capabilities and risks.

notified bodies
Notified bodies are designated organizations that assess and validate compliance of high-risk AI systems with the legal requirements set forth in regulations.<SEP>Notified bodies are designated organizations that assess compliance and safety of high-risk AI systems as part of regulatory frameworks.<SEP>Notified bodies are organizations active in the conformity assessment procedures, which the Commission coordinates.<SEP>Notified bodies are organizations designated by Member States to evaluate compliance with regulations and facilitate market access for various providers.

notifying authority
Notifying authorities are responsible for ensuring that bodies they notify participate in sector groups and assessments.

AI Regulatory Sandboxes
AI Regulatory Sandboxes are controlled environments designed to facilitate the testing and experimentation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and applications. They enable small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), start-ups, and other innovators to develop and validate their AI technologies while ensuring compliance with pertinent regulations and data protection laws. These frameworks promote innovation and cooperation among relevant stakeholders by allowing for regulatory supervision during the testing phases. By providing a structured setting for AI development, AI Regulatory Sandboxes not only help innovators navigate complex regulatory landscapes but also support the responsible advancement of AI technologies.<SEP>AI Regulatory Sandboxes are controlled environments established to foster innovation and facilitate the development, testing, and validation of innovative AI systems before they are placed on the market.<SEP>AI Regulatory Sandboxes are frameworks established to facilitate the development and testing of AI systems while ensuring compliance with regulations and fostering innovation.<SEP>AI regulatory sandboxes are controlled environments created to test innovative AI technologies under regulatory supervision to foster compliance and innovation.

Start-ups
Start-ups are a subset of SMEs that are new or emerging businesses, often characterized by innovation and growth potential.<SEP>Start-ups are newly established businesses, often in the technology sector, focused on innovation and growth.<SEP>Start-ups are newly established companies that often focus on innovative ideas and technologies, which can greatly benefit from AI regulatory sandboxes to ensure compliance and accelerate market access.<SEP>Start-ups are new businesses represented in the advisory forum, contributing innovative perspectives to the implementation of the Regulation.

Deployers
Deployers are entities or individuals responsible for implementing and using AI systems in various contexts while adhering to the specified instructions.<SEP>Deployers are entities, which can be individuals or organizations, responsible for implementing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in practical applications. They often handle high-risk AI systems and are tasked with understanding their operational context to ensure compliance with relevant regulations. Deployers may partner with AI system providers to participate in regulatory initiatives known as AI regulatory sandboxes. Additionally, they have the responsibility of conducting impact assessments on these systems. Overall, Deployers play a crucial role in the deployment and regulation of AI technology, ensuring that it is used safely and effectively in various capacities.

Local Public Authorities
Local Public Authorities are governmental entities at the municipal or regional levels considered in the guidelines for AI regulation.<SEP>Local public authorities are government bodies at the municipal level that may provide assistance and resources to SMEs and start-ups regarding the AI regulations.

Standardisation Development Process
The standardisation development process involves creating guidelines and standards for the implementation and operation of AI systems within the regulatory framework.

Board
The Board is a governing body dedicated to overseeing the regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) within the framework established by Member States. It plays a vital role in coordinating activities among national competent authorities regarding AI regulations and works closely with the AI Office to ensure the effective implementation of codes of practice and adherence to relevant regulations concerning AI.

Composed of representatives from various Member States, the Board promotes cooperation and regulatory compliance among market surveillance authorities. It is recognized as the European Artificial Intelligence Board and is committed to fostering a cohesive regulatory landscape across Member States. The Board not only monitors and evaluates the effectiveness of codes of practice but also ensures accountability among all participants involved in AI development and deployment. It solicits independent technical and scientific advice from the Union AI Testing Support Structures and other entities as required, enabling informed compliance decisions related to AI.

Additionally, the Board provides guidance and support to national competent authorities and the European Commission, ensuring adherence to best practices in the regulation of AI. It is involved in preparing agendas that align with existing regulations and procedural rules, and it oversees the activities of the Advisory Forum, from which it may solicit written contributions and opinions.

Through its comprehensive approach—including the processing of information on fines imposed under legal articles and insights from market surveillance authorities—the Board is an essential entity in the regulatory and advisory landscape, guiding the development of standardized templates and regulations while also playing a key role in the evaluation and assessment of AI models. Overall, the Board is instrumental in ensuring compliance with regulatory practices for AI and in coordinating collaboration among multiple stakeholders within the AI ecosystem.

Operators
Operators are defined as individuals or entities that bear the responsibility for adhering to regulations governing various applications of artificial intelligence (AI) systems within the Union. These operators can include those who manage or utilize high-risk AI systems, providing digital products or services, and must remain compliant with relevant regulatory obligations. They play a crucial role in the value chain, encompassing various stakeholders such as importers, distributors, and others involved in ensuring compliance.

As part of their responsibilities, operators can be subject to fines and other penalties for any non-compliance with these regulations. This underscores the necessity for operators to maintain a comprehensive awareness and understanding of the legal framework governing AI systems to effectively manage compliance and mitigate risks associated with regulatory violations. In summary, operators are key players in the AI landscape, tasked with both the operational and legal aspects of utilizing technology within regulated environments.

Communication Campaigns
Communication campaigns are organized efforts aiming to raise awareness about the obligations arising from the Regulation for operators.

Best Practices
Best Practices represent the ideal procedures and standards that the AI Office evaluates and promotes in public procurement related to AI systems.

2024/1689/oj
The reference 2024/1689/oj appears to denote a specific classification or identifier, potentially related to documents or records, though no detailed context is given.

Workplace
The workplace is a context where the use of AI systems to detect emotional states may lead to detrimental treatment of individuals due to the imbalance of power.

Education
Education is another context where AI systems could be implemented to assess emotional states, necessitating careful consideration of ethical implications.<SEP>Education refers to the systematic process of acquiring knowledge, skills, and competences necessary for individual and societal development.

Therapeutical Use
Therapeutical use refers to the application of AI systems in medical settings, which is considered acceptable and not covered by the proposed prohibitions.

Intrusive Technologies
Intrusive technologies refer to tools or systems that encroach on personal rights and freedoms, particularly with respect to identifying personal emotions and intentions.

Discriminatory Outcomes
Discriminatory Outcomes relate to negative consequences faced by individuals or groups as a result of biased social scoring practices by AI systems.<SEP>Discriminatory outcomes are negative consequences that may arise from using AI systems to assess emotions, impacting certain groups or individuals unfavorably.

Rights and Freedoms
Rights and freedoms encompass the basic entitlements of individuals, potentially compromised by intrusive technologies like AI biometric identification.<SEP>Rights and freedoms refer to the entitlements individuals have regarding personal privacy, autonomy, and protection from discrimination.

Article 60
Article 60 is a comprehensive regulatory provision that governs the deployment and operation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, with a particular focus on ensuring public safety. It outlines specific requirements and guidelines for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions, ensuring that these systems comply with established safety standards. The article details testing procedures that must be followed to achieve compliance, emphasizing the importance of safety in the operation of such technologies.

Additionally, Article 60 addresses the issue of informed consent, establishing guidelines for obtaining consent from subjects involved in the testing process under real-world conditions. This provision ensures that ethical considerations are upheld while testing AI systems. Furthermore, Article 60 encompasses requirements related to information management and access pertaining to the EU Database, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for the responsible deployment of AI technologies.

Union-wide Unique Single Identification Number
This refers to a specific identification number assigned to the testing under Article 60, ensuring traceability and accountability.

Subjects of Testing
Subjects of testing refer to individuals who participate in the testing process and must provide informed consent before involvement.

Legal Representative
A legal representative is an entity or individual appointed by a provider of AI systems to ensure compliance with EU regulations and to act on their behalf.<SEP>The legal representative refers to an individual who may act on behalf of the subjects of testing, particularly in matters related to informed consent.

Real World Conditions
Real World Conditions refer to the practical environment in which AI system testing occurs, focusing on realistic usage and impact assessment.<SEP>Real world conditions pertain to the actual circumstances under which the testing is conducted, emphasizing practical applicability and realism in the testing scenario.<SEP>Real World Conditions refer to the practical environments in which AI systems are tested for efficacy and compliance before deployment.

Informed Consent
Informed Consent is a crucial principle in AI testing that mandates participants to voluntarily agree to the testing protocols after being fully educated about the implications of their participation. It encompasses a legal acknowledgment from subjects, allowing them to partake in the testing while retaining the right to withdraw their consent at any time. The process involves informing participants about various aspects of the testing, including associated risks and objectives, ensuring that they understand what their involvement entails.

Informed Consent emphasizes the importance of clear communication and understanding, particularly when it comes to the handling of personal data. It is especially relevant in contexts involving vulnerable populations, where participants must be adequately prepared to make informed decisions about their participation. Overall, Informed Consent is designed to protect the rights and autonomy of individuals by ensuring they are well-informed and agree willingly to participate in AI system testing.

Testing Arrangements
Testing arrangements refer to the organizational and procedural aspects that govern how testing in real world conditions will be performed.

Article 94
Article 94 outlines procedural guarantees relevant to the Commission's powers and enforcement mechanisms.

Article 75(3)
Article 75(3) pertains to provisions regarding market surveillance authorities and their relationship with the Commission.

Chapter V
Chapter V discusses the powers and responsibilities of the Commission in relation to implementing regulations.<SEP>Chapter V is a section of the Regulation, set to apply starting on 2 August 2025.<SEP>Chapter V of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 sets out obligations for standardisation, particularly regarding high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI models.

AI Regulatory Sandbox
The AI Regulatory Sandbox is a structured framework established by competent authorities to create a controlled environment for the development, testing, and validation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. This environment is specifically designed to facilitate innovation in AI technologies while ensuring compliance with relevant legal and regulatory requirements. By allowing businesses and developers to experiment with high-risk AI applications under regulatory supervision, the sandbox promotes a balanced approach to exploring AI's capabilities while protecting personal data rights and public interests.

In this controlled setting, the AI Regulatory Sandbox enables stakeholders to effectively evaluate and manage potential risks associated with AI systems before their full deployment. The initiative serves as a crucial tool for both policymakers and developers, as it fosters collaborative exploration and provides valuable insights into implementation and best practices. By maintaining focus on regulatory adherence, the AI Regulatory Sandbox strives to support innovative advancements in AI while safeguarding compliance with established laws and frameworks.

Article 58
Article 58 outlines the provisions for AI systems being tested within an AI regulatory sandbox, detailing the surveillance and compliance requirements.

Article 61
Article 61 addresses additional compliance requirements related to AI systems, which market surveillance authorities must verify.<SEP>Article 61 establishes the requirements for informed consent from subjects being tested with AI systems.

Prospective Provider
Prospective Providers are individuals or entities interested in testing AI systems and must adhere to regulatory requirements during their testing process.<SEP>The prospective provider is an entity that manages the sandbox and conducts operations related to personal data processing within it.<SEP>The Prospective Provider refers to individuals or entities interested in accessing or contributing information to the EU Database.<SEP>The Prospective Provider refers to an entity that may be involved in deploying AI systems and participates in the planning and execution of testing in real-world conditions.

Serious Incident
A Serious Incident refers to significant occurrences that may compromise the testing of AI systems, prompting intervention from market surveillance authorities.<SEP>A serious incident refers to a significant occurrence that must be reported by providers or deployers of AI systems when they become aware of it.<SEP>A serious incident refers to any event related to high-risk AI systems that requires reporting to the market surveillance authorities.

Decision
A Decision made by market surveillance authorities can lead to actions affecting the testing of AI systems, including suspensions or modifications.<SEP>The Decision refers to the formal ruling made by the Market Surveillance Authority regarding a provider or prospective provider's compliance.

Article 60(4)
Article 60(4) outlines provisions regarding decisions or objections related to market surveillance in AI systems, specifically on the process of communicating grounds.

Objection
The Objection pertains to a formal challenge against the Decision made by the Market Surveillance Authority, including specific grounds for challenge.

Testing Plan
The Testing Plan outlines the procedures and requirements for evaluating AI systems by relevant authorities, including the Market Surveillance Authority.

Risk Assessments
Risk Assessments involve the evaluation of potential risks associated with AI systems, particularly in law enforcement contexts.<SEP>Risk assessments involve evaluating the potential risk of individuals committing criminal offenses based on AI profiling and personal characteristics.<SEP>Risk assessments relate to the evaluation procedures for determining the likelihood of individuals or entities engaging in criminal activities based on various characteristics and behaviors.

Customs Authorities
Customs authorities are governmental agencies responsible for regulating the flow of goods and ensuring compliance with national laws regarding imports and exports.

Actual Behaviour
Actual behaviour refers to the real-life actions of natural persons, which should be the basis for their assessment in legal contexts.

AI-Predicted Behaviour
AI-predicted behaviour is based on algorithms and profiling, potentially leading to biases in assessing natural persons.

Profiling
Profiling involves assessing individuals based on traits and characteristics, which raises ethical and legal concerns about fairness in judgement.

Objective Verifiable Facts
Objective verifiable facts are concrete evidence used to assess the involvement of natural persons in criminal activities.

Human Assessment
Human assessment refers to the evaluation of individuals by people, emphasizing the need for personal judgment in legal decisions.

Financial Fraud
Financial fraud refers to illegal acts involving the deceit or misrepresentation of financial information, often subjected to AI analysis for risk prediction.

Narcotics
Narcotics refer to illegal drugs whose distribution and localization can be analyzed by customs authorities using risk analytics.

Illicit Goods
Illicit goods encompass any products whose transaction is illegal, necessitating assessments by authorities to prevent trafficking.

Known Trafficking Routes
Known trafficking routes are established pathways used for the smuggling of illegal goods, which can be monitored using AI systems.

Regulations (EU) 2017/745
Regulations (EU) 2017/745 pertains to the regulation of medical devices and sets out requirements for their conformity assessment.

Regulations (EU) 2017/746
Regulations (EU) 2017/746 deals with in-vitro diagnostic medical devices, defining conformity assessment criteria.

Expert Panels
Expert Panels are specialized groups that evaluate and provide advice concerning medical devices under EU regulations.

Expert Laboratories
Expert Laboratories conduct testing and validation of medical devices, playing a critical role in conformity assessment processes.

Reference Laboratories
Reference Laboratories serve as authoritative entities for testing medical devices and ensuring compliance with EU standards.

Medical Devices
Medical Devices are instruments, apparatus, or machines used in healthcare that require regulatory compliance, including high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Medical Devices are products used for medical purposes, including diagnostics and therapeutic functions, regulated under EU laws.

European Human-Centric Approach to AI
The European Human-Centric Approach to AI emphasizes the development of artificial intelligence technologies that respect and enhance human rights and public interests.

Union Legal Framework
The Union legal framework refers to the set of harmonized rules established by the Union to regulate artificial intelligence and ensure public safety and rights.

Digital Transformation
Digital transformation refers to the broad societal and economic changes driven by the adoption of digital technologies, including AI.

Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs)
SMEs are businesses whose personnel numbers fall below certain limits and are emphasized within the union's regulations for their role in innovation and economic growth.

Innovation Measures
Innovation measures refer to actions and strategies put in place to promote the creation and growth of new technologies within the Union, particularly AI.

recommendations to the Commission on a framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies
This category outlines the ethical considerations proposed by the European Parliament for the development and regulation of artificial intelligence and robotic technologies.

October 2020
October 2020 refers to the time frame during which significant discussions and resolutions took place in the European Parliament regarding technology ethics.

Risk Management System
A Risk Management System is a framework organizations use to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with their high-risk AI systems.<SEP>A Risk Management System refers to a systematic approach intended to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with high-risk AI systems throughout their lifecycle.<SEP>The Risk Management System is a framework established to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with high-risk AI systems.

Article 13
Article 13 encompasses several significant details regarding the obligations and guidelines related to the processing of personal data and the deployment of high-risk AI systems within the framework of EU regulations. Specifically, Article 13 is part of Directive (EU) 2016/680, which outlines requirements for law enforcement concerning personal data handling. 

Additionally, Article 13 mandates that deployers of high-risk AI systems must meet specific information and training requirements. It emphasizes the necessity for providers to supply relevant information that allows for proper assessments of these AI systems. Furthermore, Article 13 details the regulations surrounding the testing and usage of AI systems, ensuring that they comply with data protection laws. Overall, Article 13 serves as a critical regulatory requirement that supports the effective and compliant integration of AI technologies, particularly in high-risk scenarios, ensuring that personal data is handled responsibly.

Identification and Analysis of Risks
The process of identifying and analyzing known and reasonably foreseeable risks associated with High-Risk AI Systems, focusing on their impact on health, safety, or fundamental rights.

Estimation and Evaluation of Risks
The process of estimating and evaluating potential risks that may arise during the use of High-Risk AI Systems, including misuse scenarios.

Risk Management Measures
Risk Management Measures refer to strategies and actions adopted to mitigate or eliminate identified risks associated with High-Risk AI Systems.<SEP>Risk Management Measures refer to structured approaches to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Risk Management Measures refer to the strategies and procedures established to minimize and manage potential risks associated with high-risk AI systems, ensuring they operate safely and effectively.

Technical Information
Technical Information refers to data or guidance provided to aid in the safe deployment and operation of High-Risk AI Systems, crucial for mitigating risks.

Residual Risk
Residual Risk is the remaining risk after risk management measures have been implemented for high-risk AI systems.

Hazards
Hazards represent potential sources of harm or adverse effects that need to be evaluated in the context of high-risk AI systems.

Technical Knowledge
Technical Knowledge refers to the expertise and understanding necessary to effectively deploy and manage high-risk AI systems.

European Union Law
European Union Law encompasses the legal framework governing various activities within the EU, including legislation pertaining to AI systems and ethical research.<SEP>European Union Law encompasses the rules, regulations, and directives that govern the member states of the European Union, ensuring mutual legal standards and operational integration.<SEP>European Union Law refers to a set of legal regulations and directives applicable within member states that govern various sectors, including artificial intelligence testing and risk management.

Vulnerable Groups
Vulnerable Groups refer to specific populations that may be disproportionately affected by the deployment and operation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. These groups are characterized by a higher risk of experiencing adverse impacts due to socio-economic factors, necessitating special consideration and protection under regulations. Vulnerable Groups include segments of the population such as minors, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities, all of whom may face greater threats from AI systems. Additionally, these groups may require additional safeguards in light of their susceptibility to risk, particularly during the testing of AI systems. Overall, Vulnerable Groups encompass those who might be affected differently by the advancements and implications of AI technology.<SEP>Vulnerable groups are individuals who may face higher risks and ethical considerations during testing due to their circumstances or status.<SEP>Vulnerable groups include individuals who require special consideration during testing due to their age or disability, ensuring their rights and protections.<SEP>Vulnerable groups include populations that face systemic discrimination and bias, often including racial or ethnic minorities that may be adversely affected by AI decision-making.<SEP>Vulnerable groups refer to populations that may be at risk of discrimination or negative impacts from AI systems, including racial or ethnic minorities.

Moreover, the panel integrates input from the scientific community into the regulation and governance frameworks surrounding AI, ensuring that scientific perspectives are incorporated in discussions and decisions. Through its various roles, the Scientific Panel aims to promote informed and responsible AI development while addressing the challenges posed by emerging technologies.

Members
Members are individuals who comprise the scientific panel, responsible for issuing alerts and executing tasks.

Regulatory Compliance
Regulatory Compliance refers to the adherence to laws, regulations, guidelines, and specifications relevant to business processes and activities, particularly concerning high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Regulatory compliance involves adhering to laws and regulations that govern the operation and safety of AI systems and products.

Design Control
Design Control refers to the systematic procedures used to manage the development and modifications of high-risk AI systems, ensuring they meet regulatory standards.

European Union Regulation
European Union Regulation encompasses the legal framework governing the implementation and monitoring of high-risk AI systems across member states.

Data Filtration
Data Filtration refers to the process of filtering and managing data to ensure its quality and relevance before being applied to high-risk AI systems.

Data Mining
Data Mining is the practice of analyzing and extracting valuable information from large data sets, crucial for the operation of AI systems.

Data Aggregation
Data Aggregation is the collection and compilation of data from various sources into a single format for analysis and operational purposes in AI.

Data Retention
Data Retention involves storing data over a specified period, ensuring compliance with regulations for high-risk AI systems.

Customers
Customers are the end-users or clients who interact with high-risk AI systems, having an interest in the systems' safety and efficacy.

Interested Parties
Interested Parties are any stakeholders who have a vested interest in the performance and regulation of high-risk AI systems.

Transparency Requirements
Transparency Requirements pertain to the obligations of AI system providers and deployers to ensure understanding of the system's functionality and risks before it is used.

Instructions for Use
Instructions for Use are comprehensive guidelines provided by the Provider that encompass essential information for the safe and effective operation of high-risk AI systems. These instructions detail the characteristics, functionalities, and limitations of the AI systems, aimed at assisting deployers in their implementation. They highlight the obligations and intended uses of the systems, ensuring users understand the proper usage protocols. Specifically, Instructions for Use include critical risk considerations that are vital for safe operation, thereby ensuring users are well-informed about the intended purpose and functionality of the AI systems they are utilizing.

Target Deployers
Target Deployers are the intended users of the AI system who must understand the instructions for use and their obligations.

Technical Robustness
Technical Robustness is the quality that high-risk AI systems should possess to ensure they are resilient against errors, faults, and unexpected situations.

Technical Measures
Technical Measures are actions taken to design and develop AI systems to prevent undesirable behavior and ensure their robustness.<SEP>Technical Measures refer to the specific strategies and tools applied by deployers to ensure the proper functionality and compliance of high-risk AI systems.

Organizational Measures
Organizational Measures involve practices within organizations that enhance the reliability and safety of AI systems.

Fail-Safe Plans
Fail-Safe Plans are mechanisms within AI systems that allow for safe interruption of operation during anomalies or boundary breaches.

Errors
Errors refer to mistakes or faults that may occur in AI systems, potentially leading to harmful outcomes if not mitigated.

Faults
Faults are defects or failures in a system that can disrupt the proper functioning of AI systems, necessitating robust measures to address them.

Inconsistencies
Inconsistencies are discrepancies that may arise in the behavior or outputs of AI systems, contributing to risks if not carefully managed.

Unexpected Situations
Unexpected Situations refer to unforeseen circumstances that can impact the performance of AI systems, requiring built-in safety protocols.

Harmful Behavior
Harmful Behavior encompasses negative actions or outputs resulting from AI systems that can adversely affect users or stakeholders.

Undesirable Behavior
Undesirable Behavior includes actions or outputs from AI systems that, while not necessarily harmful, may not align with user expectations or ethical standards.

Data Minimisation
Data minimisation is a principle requiring that only necessary personal data be collected and processed to reduce risks to privacy.

data.entity_name: Data Protection by Design and by Default
data.content:
Data Protection by Design and by Default
Data protection by design and by default is a principle aimed at integrating data protection measures into the development of technologies and processes from the outset.

Anonymisation and Encryption
Anonymisation and encryption are security measures employed to protect personal data by making it unidentifiable or unreadable.

Anonymisation
Anonymisation is a technique used to remove identifiable information from personal data sets, thereby protecting individuals' identities and privacy.

Encryption
Encryption is a method of converting information or data into a code to prevent unauthorized access, ensuring that sensitive data remains confidential during processing.

Data Governance
Data governance refers to the overall management of the availability, usability, integrity, and security of data employed within AI systems, ensuring compliance with relevant regulations.<SEP>Data governance refers to the overall management of the availability, usability, integrity, and security of the data employed in an organization, ensuring compliance with relevant laws and regulations.

Third Countries
Third Countries are nations outside the European Union that enter into international agreements with the Union or Member States for cooperation.<SEP>Third countries are nations outside the Union that do not operate under the Union's legal and regulatory framework but interact with it via market activities.

free and open-source licence
Free and open-source licences are legal terms that permit access, usage, modification, and distribution of software, including AI models.

provider
The provider is an entity, which can be a natural or legal person, that has specific obligations under certain regulations, highlighting its role in compliance and accountability. This entity is responsible for developing and managing high-risk AI systems, ensuring that these systems comply with relevant regulations. Additionally, the provider offers or maintains general-purpose AI models and is tasked with ensuring compliance with EU regulations. The provider is also authorized to represent legal persons in matters concerning general-purpose AI models, and generally refers to individuals or organizations that supply AI systems to the market while upholding regulatory standards.

European Digital Innovation Hubs
European Digital Innovation Hubs are entities that play a crucial role in fostering the development and scalability of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) systems. They are designed to support the digital transformation of businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), by providing access to innovation services, funding, and resources. These institutions offer expertise and resources that assist organizations in integrating advanced technologies such as AI and other digital innovations. Additionally, European Digital Innovation Hubs aim to support providers and notified bodies by facilitating compliance with market requirements and delivering specialized knowledge in the field.

AI System Providers
AI System Providers are entities that place AI systems on the market or put them into service, regardless of their location.<SEP>AI system providers are entities that apply for participation in the AI regulatory sandboxes, subject to eligibility and selection criteria.<SEP>AI system providers are entities that develop and supply AI technologies capable of generating or manipulating media content.

Relevant Actors
Relevant actors within the AI ecosystem include stakeholders like researchers, testing facilities, and standardization organizations that support the operation of AI regulatory sandboxes.

Conformity Assessment Obligations
Conformity assessment obligations are requirements that AI system providers must comply with to ensure their systems meet regulatory standards.<SEP>Conformity assessment obligations refer to the requirements that organizations must meet to comply with regulatory standards, particularly in the context of AI systems.

Codes of Conduct
Codes of Conduct are guidelines developed by AI Providers to ensure ethical practices and compliance with regulations in the deployment of AI systems.<SEP>Codes of Conduct serve as guidelines for the ethical development and deployment of AI systems based on established principles.<SEP>Codes of conduct are guidelines established to ensure ethical and safe practices within the AI ecosystem, particularly for SMEs and start-ups in regulatory sandboxes.<SEP>Codes of conduct refer to voluntary guidelines that AI system providers may apply for adherence as part of their participation in the regulatory framework.

Research and Experimentation Labs
Research and Experimentation Labs are facilities dedicated to the development, testing, and validation of new technologies, including AI systems.<SEP>Research and experimentation labs are facilities focused on the development and testing of new technologies and methodologies in AI research.

Start-Ups
Start-Ups are newly established businesses, often focused on innovative products or services, and are typically in the early stages of development.<SEP>Start-Ups are small businesses that may develop innovative AI systems and are supported through access to AI regulatory sandboxes to enter the Union market.<SEP>Start-ups are newly established businesses that often focus on innovative products or services and face unique challenges in regulatory compliance, particularly in emerging fields like AI.

Testing and Experimentation Facilities
Testing and Experimentation Facilities provide environments and systems for rigorously evaluating the performance and compliance of AI technologies.<SEP>Testing and experimentation facilities provide the infrastructure needed to assess and validate new technologies, including AI systems, in controlled environments.<SEP>Testing and experimentation facilities refer to environments where AI systems can be safely tested and assessed for compliance with regulatory standards.

data.entity_name: Learning Outcomes of AI Regulatory Sandboxes
data.content:
Learning Outcomes of AI Regulatory Sandboxes
Learning outcomes of AI regulatory sandboxes refer to the insights and knowledge gained from testing AI systems, which can inform compliance and best practices.

Guidance on Implementation
Guidance on implementation refers to informational resources provided to help organizations comply with laws and regulations, particularly in AI and data protection.

Standardisation Documents
Standardisation documents are official guidelines and protocols that facilitate compliance and consistency in regulatory practices across organizations and industries.

Centres of Excellence
Centres of Excellence are specialized institutions that promote best practices and knowledge transfer in areas such as technology and innovation.

authorities
The authorities refer to governing bodies or organizations responsible for enforcing laws and regulations within the Union.

Open-Source AI Models
Open-source AI models are versions of AI systems that are publicly available for use and modification, which may pose challenges for risk compliance post-release.

Training Process
The training process involves allocating compute resources and planning to develop AI models, which is critical in determining their capabilities and risks.

Compute Resources
Compute resources refer to the technical infrastructure (such as CPUs and GPUs) required for the training and operation of AI models.

Presumption of Systemic Risk
The presumption of systemic risk occurs when a general-purpose AI model meets certain thresholds indicating high-impact capabilities.

open-source model
The open-source model refers to a software development approach where the source code is made publicly available for use, modification, and distribution.

Compliance Measures
Compliance measures are procedures and actions taken to ensure adherence to regulations and laws.

Conformity Assessment Procedures
Conformity Assessment Procedures are evaluative processes to ensure that high-risk AI systems meet established safety, health, and environmental standards before they can be authorized.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Procedures refer to the processes involved in evaluating whether AI systems comply with established regulations, particularly those deemed high-risk.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Procedures are processes that ensure products comply with specific requirements before they can be sold in the market.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Procedures are methods and standards that ensure AI systems meet required specifications before certification.<SEP>Conformity assessment procedures are systematic processes outlined in regulations to evaluate the compliance of high-risk AI systems with established standards.

Commission Expert Groups
Commission expert groups are gatherings of experts involved in the preparation of delegated acts for the European Union.

Expert Groups
Expert Groups are collaborative bodies comprised of experts who assist in the preparation and evaluation of delegated acts for the European Commission.<SEP>Expert Groups consist of professionals providing advice and developing expertise in specific fields, such as product safety and cybersecurity within the Union context.

Regulation for AI Models
The Regulation for AI Models outlines specific obligations and rules governing the provision and integration of general-purpose AI models within the market.

Developers of AI Models
Developers of AI Models are responsible for integrating general-purpose AI models into systems and must comply with regulations when these models are marketed.

Obligations for Providers of AI Models
Obligations for Providers of AI Models refer to the legal responsibilities that developers must adhere to when placing their models in the market.

Components of AI Systems
Components of AI Systems include all necessary elements that work together with AI models to create functional AI applications.

User Interface
The User Interface is a crucial component that allows users to interact with AI systems, enhancing usability and accessibility.

Systemic Risks of AI Models
Systemic Risks of AI Models refer to potential negative consequences that could arise from the deployment of certain AI models in the market.

Data Training Methods
Data Training Methods encompass the techniques such as self-supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning used to develop general-purpose AI models.

Market Integration of AI Models

Initial Model Usage for Research

Provider of General-Purpose AI Model

Own Model

Internal Processes

Regulatory Obligations
Regulatory Obligations are requirements that govern the placement and operational expectations of AI models on the market to ensure safety and compliance.

Subcontractor

Subsidiary

authorised representative

logs
Logs are automatically generated records by a high-risk AI system that provide data for compliance and safety verification.

certificate
A certificate is an official document that confirms that a provider's system meets predefined standards, allowing it to operate in a particular domain.<SEP>A certificate issued by a notified body indicates compliance of a high-risk AI system with regulatory requirements.

notified body
A notified body is an authorized organization designated to assess the compliance of products and systems with regulatory standards.<SEP>A notified body refers to an organization designated to assess the compliance of high-risk AI systems and issue certificates.<SEP>The notified body is an entity involved in assessing and ensuring compliance with regulations, especially regarding terminations and mandates.<SEP>Notified bodies are organizations designated to assess and monitor compliance concerning high-risk AI systems and their associated certifications.

competent authority
Competent authorities are regulatory agencies tasked with overseeing the implementation of regulations surrounding high-risk AI systems.

Regulation Section 2
Regulation Section 2 outlines the specific requirements that high-risk AI systems must adhere to for compliance.

registration obligations
Registration obligations refer to the requirements set forth in the Regulation regarding the documentation and verification of high-risk AI systems.

market surveillance authority
Market surveillance authorities are entities responsible for monitoring compliance with laws and regulations concerning products and services in the market.<SEP>Market surveillance authorities are organizations responsible for overseeing compliance with market regulations and handling complaints.<SEP>The market surveillance authority is a national regulatory body tasked with overseeing compliance with market regulations, particularly in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. Its primary responsibilities include ensuring that entities, such as providers, adhere to legal obligations and protecting consumer rights. Additionally, the authority is specifically charged with monitoring compliance related to the use of various technologies, including biometric identification systems, in public spaces. Furthermore, it plays a key role in overseeing the compliance of high-risk AI systems with applicable legal requirements. The market surveillance authority also monitors regulations concerning AI systems and is responsible for receiving notifications of assessments from their deployers, ensuring that all market actors conform to established standards and regulations.<SEP>Market surveillance authorities are regulatory bodies responsible for monitoring products in the market to ensure compliance with safety and other regulatory standards.<SEP>The market surveillance authority is responsible for ensuring that products and services comply with regulations and standards to protect citizens.

mandate
A mandate refers to the authorization or directive given to a provider, which outlines their responsibilities and obligations under the regulation.

termination of mandate
Termination of a mandate occurs when a provider ends its obligations or responsibilities defined by the regulation, requiring notification to relevant bodies.

European Union Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Regulation (EU) 2016/679, known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), provides guidelines on the collection and processing of personal data within the EU.

European Union Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 is concerned with the protection of personal data in the EU and applies to the processing of personal data in the context of Union institutions and bodies.

Public Safety
Public Safety includes measures and policies put in place to protect the well-being and health of the public in various contexts, which can be enhanced by AI systems.

Public Health
Public Health focuses on the health of the population as a whole, including disease prevention, control, and improvement of health care systems through innovative technologies like AI.

Energy Sustainability
Energy Sustainability emphasizes the need for energy systems that meet current demands without compromising future generations, with potential AI contributions to efficiency.

Transport Systems
Transport Systems refer to the frameworks and networks that ensure efficient movement of people and goods, which can benefit from AI implementations for safety and resilience.

Data Subjects
Data Subjects are individuals whose personal data is being processed, and they have rights and protections under laws such as Directive (EU) 2016/680.<SEP>Data Subjects are individuals whose personal data is collected and processed, and their rights must be protected during AI system experimentation.

Union data protection law
Union data protection law encompasses regulations and guidelines that aim to protect personal data and the privacy of individuals within the EU.

Article 39
Article 39 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 outlines specific provisions regarding personal data processing during sandbox experimentation.

Sandbox Experimentation
Sandbox Experimentation involves the testing and experimentation of AI systems within the regulatory sandbox framework to ensure safety and compliance with laws.<SEP>Sandbox experimentation refers to a controlled environment for testing and validating innovative processes, particularly in AI systems within the frameworks of data protection law.

Data Processing Environment
Data processing environment is an isolated and secure context in which personal data can be handled according to specific regulations.

Law Enforcement Authorities
Law Enforcement Authorities are governmental agencies tasked with maintaining public order, enforcing laws, and ensuring the safety and rights of citizens. They play a critical role in preventing, detecting, investigating, and prosecuting criminal offenses. As part of their operations, these authorities may utilize high-risk AI systems to enhance their capabilities, although such systems are not covered under post-market monitoring obligations due to their operational sensitivity. Additionally, Law Enforcement Authorities may operate within AI regulatory sandboxes, enabling them to incorporate advanced technologies while adhering to regulatory standards. Overall, these agencies are integral to fostering public safety and order through a combination of traditional law enforcement practices and the innovative use of technology.<SEP>Law enforcement authorities are agencies involved in the application or use of high-risk AI systems in public safety.

Testing Results
Testing results are the outcomes derived from the evaluation of AI systems in the sandbox, providing evidence of their development and compliance.

AI regulatory sandboxes
AI regulatory sandboxes are controlled environments created by regulators to allow companies, particularly SMEs and start-ups, to test innovative AI systems under regulatory oversight before full-scale implementation.<SEP>AI regulatory sandboxes are frameworks established for the testing and validation of AI systems under controlled conditions, ensuring compliance with relevant laws and regulations.<SEP>AI regulatory sandboxes are frameworks that allow for the trial of AI technologies in a controlled environment to ensure compliance with regulations.

law enforcement authorities
Law enforcement authorities are agencies tasked with maintaining public order and enforcing laws.<SEP>Law enforcement authorities are governmental agencies responsible for the prevention and investigation of criminal offences and the enforcement of laws regarding public security.<SEP>Law enforcement authorities are mandated agencies responsible for the prevention and investigation of crime, enforcement of the law, and maintenance of public order.<SEP>Law enforcement authorities are governmental agencies responsible for the enforcement of laws, preventing crime, and maintaining public order.

personal data
Personal data encompasses any information that relates to an identified or identifiable individual, subject to data protection regulations.<SEP>Personal data refers to any information that relates to an identified or identifiable individual, particularly in the context of AI systems and their regulatory oversight.<SEP>Personal data refers to any data relating to identified or identifiable individuals, which is protected under various regulations including those mentioned.<SEP>Personal data refers to any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, which is protected under related regulations.<SEP>Personal data is defined under EU regulation as information that relates to an identified or identifiable individual.

Criminal Offences
Criminal Offences entail violations of laws that require investigation or prosecution, often necessitating the processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes.<SEP>Criminal Offences refer to illegal activities that may invoke the law, necessitating the deployment of AI systems for prevention and investigation.<SEP>Criminal offences refer to illegal activities that may require detection or intervention by AI systems under certain legal frameworks.

Processing of Personal Data
The Processing of Personal Data involves handling and analyzing data related to individuals, which is subject to legal standards in the context of AI and law enforcement activities.

natural person
A natural person is a human being, as opposed to a legal entity, involved in the application of regulations and laws.<SEP>A natural person refers to an individual human being recognized by law, and in this context, it implies that such individuals can be responsible for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Natural persons refer to individual human beings with legal rights and obligations.<SEP>A natural person refers to an individual human being who can hold editorial responsibilities for published content.

legal person
A legal person is an entity, such as a corporation or organization, that has legal rights and responsibilities distinct from those of a natural person, which can also be responsible for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Legal persons refer to entities such as corporations or organizations that have legal rights and responsibilities.<SEP>A legal person represents an organization or a corporation that has legal rights and obligations under the law.<SEP>A legal person refers to a non-human entity, such as a corporation or organization, that has legal rights and responsibilities, including editorial control.

Public Entity
Public Entity describes entities designated by Member States to perform specific tasks related to the supervision and application of the Regulation.

Recital 29
Recital 29 outlines prohibitions regarding AI practices that manipulate or deceive individuals, causing significant harm.

Recital 31
Recital 31 addresses the prohibitions related to the evaluation and classification of individuals based on social behavior or characteristics.

Recital 42
Recital 42 discusses the restrictions on using AI systems for making risk assessments based on profiling individuals for criminal activities.

Subliminal Techniques
Subliminal techniques refer to methods that operate below the threshold of conscious awareness, often used in marketing or persuasion that manipulate behavior.

Manipulative Techniques
Manipulative techniques involve strategies intentionally designed to distort perceptions or compel decisions, often causing harm to individuals or groups.

Vulnerabilities of Natural Persons
Vulnerabilities of natural persons are specific weaknesses that can be exploited due to age, disability, or socio-economic status, often leading to harmful outcomes.

Social Behavior
Social behavior entails actions performed by individuals or groups that can influence their interactions and treatment within society.<SEP>Social behavior refers to actions that individuals engage in when interacting with others, which can influence their social scoring and treatment by AI systems.

Criminal Offence Risk Assessment
Risk assessment concerning criminal offenses involves evaluating the likelihood that an individual may engage in illegal activities based on certain profiling characteristics.

Facial Recognition Databases
Facial recognition databases are collections of facial images used by AI systems for identification, often raised for concerns regarding privacy and consent.<SEP>Facial recognition databases are collections of facial images used for identification purposes, often raising concerns regarding privacy and surveillance.

Biometric Categorisation Systems
Biometric Categorisation Systems are used to categorize individuals based on biometric data, like facial recognition, to infer personal attributes.<SEP>Biometric categorisation systems are technologies that analyze biometric data to classify individuals, potentially infringing on personal rights.<SEP>Biometric categorisation systems utilize biometric data, such as faces or fingerprints, to classify individuals based on sensitive attributes like political opinions or sexual orientation.

Workplace and Education Institutions
Workplace and Education Institutions represent environments where AI systems may be applied for monitoring and assessing individuals but are subject to strict regulations.<SEP>Workplace and education institutions are environments where AI systems may be used to infer emotions, raising concerns about privacy and ethical implications.

Unfavorable Treatment
Unfavorable treatment describes the negative consequences faced by individuals based on their social scores or profiling, impacting their social interactions.

CCTV Footage
CCTV Footage consists of recorded video surveillance that captures events in public spaces, often used for security and monitoring.<SEP>CCTV footage is video surveillance that can be used to create or expand facial recognition databases, raising concerns about privacy and consent.<SEP>CCTV footage consists of video recordings captured by closed-circuit television systems, often used for security and surveillance purposes.

Human Rights
Human Rights encompass the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, which can be affected by the use of AI systems and biometric data.<SEP>Human rights encompass the fundamental rights and freedoms that belong to every person, which can be threatened by AI systems and profiling.<SEP>Human Rights refer to the principles that protect individual freedoms and ensure that AI systems do not infringe upon these rights.<SEP>Human rights refer to the fundamental rights and freedoms that every individual is entitled to, which can be jeopardized by misuse of AI technologies.

EU Regulation 2016/679
EU Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR) governs the handling of personal data within the European Union, including biometric data for law enforcement purposes.

Facial Images
Facial Images refer to pictures or visual representations of faces that can be collected from various sources, including the internet and CCTV footage, for analysis and identification.

Internet
The Internet is a global network that facilitates the exchange of information and the sharing of data, including facial images, which can be scraped for various purposes.

Emotional Inference
Emotional Inference is the process by which AI systems interpret and deduce human emotions based on analysis of data, particularly facial expressions and biometric indicators.

Abolition of Biometric Systems
The Abolition of Biometric Systems refers to discussions or regulations aiming to limit or prohibit the use of biometric categorization technologies due to privacy and ethical concerns.

Human Beings
Human Beings are individuals whose biometric data can be collected and analyzed by AI systems, often leading to privacy implications and questions of consent.

real-time remote biometric identification systems
Real-time remote biometric identification systems are technologies used for recognizing and verifying individuals' identities in public spaces for law enforcement purposes.<SEP>These systems are technology used for identifying individuals in real-time in publicly accessible spaces, specifically for law enforcement purposes.

criminal offence
Criminal offences are actions or behaviors that violate a law and are punishable by statutory law.

Annex II
Annex II refers to a specific section of regulatory legislation that outlines offenses punishable by custodial sentences that are relevant to law enforcement and biometric processing.

terrorist attack
Terrorist attacks represent acts of violence against civilians intentionally carried out to instill fear and achieve specific political objectives.

criminal investigation
Criminal investigation is a legal process conducted to uncover and gather evidence surrounding offenses committed by individuals.

crimes
Crimes are actions or behaviors that violate laws and are punishable by the state; they include various offenses as defined by legislation.

criminal penalty
A criminal penalty is a consequence assigned by a legal system in response to a criminal act, which can include imprisonment, fines, or other forms of punishment.

system

fundamental rights impact assessment

A Judicial Authority is an independent body responsible for making legal decisions and granting authorizations related to law enforcement actions, including the use of biometric identification systems.<SEP>The Judicial Authority provides legal oversight and must grant authorization for the use of real-time biometric systems in public spaces, ensuring compliance with national laws.<SEP>Judicial authorities are institutions responsible for upholding the rule of law, making legal decisions, and administering justice.<SEP>Judicial Authority refers to entities within the legal system that possess the power to make decisions on the legality of the use of AI systems in investigations.<SEP>Judicial Authority refers to the body that grants authorization for the use of high-risk AI systems in investigations, with decisions subject to judicial review.

real-time remote biometric identification system
A real-time remote biometric identification system is a technological solution utilized for identifying individuals in publicly accessible spaces, subject to legal regulations.<SEP>The real-time remote biometric identification system is a technology used for identifying individuals in publicly accessible spaces, particularly for law enforcement purposes.<SEP>A type of remote biometric identification system that performs identification instantly or with minimal delays to prevent circumvention.<SEP>This system identifies individuals almost instantaneously by processing biometric data through a comparison system, allowing for minimal delays.

authorization

data retention policies

national law

National Data Protection Authorities are governmental entities that oversee the compliance of data protection laws, particularly related to personal data processing in AI systems.<SEP>National Data Protection Authorities oversee compliance with data protection laws and regulations, especially in relation to AI systems processing personal data.<SEP>National data protection authorities are bodies responsible for enforcing data protection laws and regulations in their respective countries.<SEP>These are independent public authorities in Member States that protect personal data and privacy, ensuring compliance with data protection laws.

Recitals 37, 38, 39, 40, and 41
These recitals provide context and additional details regarding the regulation of biometric identification systems.

Data Protection Authorities
Data Protection Authorities are entities responsible for overseeing compliance with data protection laws, ensuring that personal data is handled according to legal standards.<SEP>Data Protection Authorities are specialized governmental bodies that oversee compliance with data protection regulations, safeguarding individuals’ data privacy rights.

AI Practice

Annual Reports on Biometric Systems

Compliance Regulation

Required Information

Written Mandate

Representative

Three Years

Sub-groups

Chair
The Chair is a representative from the Member States responsible for leading the Board and coordinating its activities.<SEP>The Chair is the individual responsible for leading the Board's activities and ensuring effective operation of meetings.

Stakeholders
Stakeholders are individuals or groups that possess a vested interest or concern in the development, deployment, and regulation of AI systems. This diverse group includes a wide range of parties such as providers and users of AI technology, industry representatives, national authorities, market participants, academia, civil society, and various advocacy groups, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), consumer organizations, and environmental advocates. 

Stakeholders play a crucial role in the standardization of AI practices and are instrumental in promoting ethical considerations in the development of AI technologies. They engage actively in the implementation and application of regulations, especially concerning high-risk AI systems, where their interests encompass not only organizations and users but also regulatory bodies. Furthermore, stakeholders participate in AI regulatory sandboxes, collaborating with businesses, innovators, and regulatory entities to explore and implement AI technologies effectively.

Additionally, stakeholders include experts who are invited to partake in forums and meetings related to AI governance and development, thus ensuring that the implementation of AI policies and regulations reflects diverse perspectives and interests from across all sectors of society. Overall, stakeholders are integral to the ongoing dialogue around AI, involved in shaping and implementing standards and policies that govern AI technologies.

advisory forum
The advisory forum consists of stakeholders that provide advice and recommendations during the standardisation process for AI.<SEP>The advisory forum is established to provide technical expertise and advice to the Board and the Commission on AI-related tasks, representing a balanced selection of stakeholders from diverse sectors.<SEP>The advisory forum is mentioned as a consultative body that may provide input and oversight on the activities of the Board via invited representatives.<SEP>The advisory forum mentioned refers to a consultative body that the Commission consults when drafting common specifications and implementing acts.

notifying authorities
Notifying authorities are entities that communicate relevant information about compliance and market practices to the Board and other bodies within this regulatory framework.

Affected Person

Union Law Exceptions
Union Law Exceptions encompass the specific legal provisions that may permit deviations or exceptions to the obligations placed on deployers of AI systems.

Union AI Testing Support Structures
Union AI testing support structures are designated organizations responsible for performing tasks and providing technical or scientific advice as per EU regulations on AI.

Union market
The Union market refers to the collective market of the European Union where businesses operate and provide goods and services, including AI models.

providers
Providers are entities or businesses that place general-purpose AI models on the Union market, ensuring compliance with relevant regulations and obligations.<SEP>Providers refer to entities or organizations that offer general-purpose AI models and must comply with the established codes of practice.<SEP>Providers are entities that develop or distribute products containing AI systems and are responsible for ensuring regulatory compliance.<SEP>Providers refer to the entities involved in supplying high-risk AI systems and services, ensuring safe and reliable AI applications.

copyright and related rights

Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790
Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 outlines specific obligations for providers concerning the reservation of rights by rightsholders.<SEP>This article outlines specific obligations regarding copyright compliance and the reservation of rights within the context of AI model training and usage in the EU.

Articles 53 and 55
Articles 53 and 55 refer to specific provisions within regulations that outline obligations related to the use of AI models and systemic risk management.<SEP>Articles 53 and 55 specify the obligations that must be adhered to by providers of general-purpose AI models within the Union.

Civil Society Organizations
Civil Society Organizations are non-governmental entities that can contribute to the drawing up of codes of practice and ensure diverse stakeholder involvement in AI regulations.<SEP>Civil society organizations play a crucial role in advocating for individuals' rights and participating in fundamental rights impact assessments.

Academia
Academia encompasses educational institutions and scholars contributing research and perspectives on the ethical implications of AI technologies.<SEP>Academia includes educational and research institutions that contribute expertise and knowledge in the formulation of codes of conduct for AI systems.<SEP>Academia refers to educational institutions and researchers that can provide insights and support in the development of AI-related codes of practice.<SEP>Academia involves educational institutions and scholars who bring research and theoretical insights regarding the Regulation.

codes of practice
Codes of practice are guidelines that providers of AI models can use to demonstrate compliance with legal obligations under AI regulations.<SEP>Codes of practice are specific guidelines established to ensure that the use of general-purpose AI models adheres to safety, ethical, and legal standards.

key performance indicators
Key performance indicators are measurable values used to evaluate the success of the codes of practice in achieving their objectives.

2 May 2025
2 May 2025 is the date by which codes of practice for AI providers must be established to ensure compliance with the regulation.<SEP>2 May 2025 is the deadline set for the finalization of the codes of practice related to AI usage within the Union.

Article 55
Article 55 includes additional obligations that providers must follow under the regulatory framework governing AI.<SEP>Article 55 may relate to compliance aspects within the same legal governance of AI models.

May 2025
May 2025 is the deadline by which codes of practice should be finalized according to the regulations set forth in the implementing acts.

August 2025
